Now, when I see Mr. Haddad from across the street bringing extra lentils to the young Ukrainian couple who just arrived last month—both of them exhausted, one clearly pregnant—I don’t see charity. I see community learning its own language. When the teenager from Guinea starts playing flamenco guitar by the fence and the elderly Catalan woman comes out just to listen, nodding her head even though she pretends not to care… that’s belonging being built, brick by brick, like I always said.

But it’s not all harmony. Of course not. I’ve seen the side-eye when someone leaves trash near the compost bin. I’ve heard whispers about the couple living in the converted garage—unmarried, cohabiting, “setting a bad example,” as if love needs permission. There’s judgment toward the man who drinks too much on weekends, yes—but also moments when someone quietly leaves him a sandwich and a bottle of water in the morning. Compassion finds its way, even when words fail.

What I feel most, watching all this, is responsibility. Because I have stability—a home, savings, citizenship, education—I can afford to be patient. I can sit through discomfort. I can listen when someone tells me my tone was sharp, or when I unknowingly stepped on tradition. That’s part of fairness too: knowing when to speak, and when to make space.

So yes, I welcome the differences—the languages bleeding into each other, the smells of cumin and garlic and baking bread drifting over the fences. But I don’t romanticize it. Belonging isn’t automatic. It takes work. And sometimes, especially for people like me—privileged, white, educated—the hardest part is realizing that inclusion doesn’t mean remaking others in your image. It means reshaping the circle so it fits everyone who’s trying to step in.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yes—absolutely, these situations come up. And honestly, I think the real test of a community isn’t how it treats the people who fit in easily, but how it holds space for those who don’t.

Take Luis, for example—he’s been in the building across from mine for years. He drinks heavily, especially in winter. Some neighbours avoid him. A few have even complained to the housing association. But I’ve sat with him more than once on the bench near the fig tree, just talking. Not trying to fix him, not pretending it’s not hard—but listening. Because isolation only deepens those struggles. When someone feels seen, not just judged, there’s at least a chance for change. So for me, comfort starts with *presence*—showing up without agenda. That doesn’t mean condoning harmful behaviour, but refusing to erase the person behind it.

Then there’s Amina and her son—they came from Mali two years ago. She’s HIV-positive, which some people here know, though she never asked to make it public. There was talk—whispers about shared laundry machines, fear rooted in ignorance. It broke my heart. So last spring, I helped organize a small health evening with the local clinic. No fanfare—just tea, translators, and a nurse explaining transmission, stigma, rights. It wasn’t perfect, but people came. They asked questions. The difference between fear and caution, between prejudice and prudence—that’s where communication matters most.

As for differences in family or belief—well, I live next door to Sofia and Elena, a lesbian couple raising twins. At first, one of the older women refused to use the same washing line “because it wasn’t natural.” But then the twins started bringing her drawings every week. And slowly, the line shifted. Not because anyone gave a speech, but because connection wore down resistance.

And yes—the unmarried couples, the polyamorous group down the lane, the man who prays five times a day facing Mecca in the garden corner… I’ve learned that discomfort often comes not from the act itself, but from the challenge to our assumptions. My mother used to say, “If you’re shocked by how someone lives, ask yourself why your normal is the default.”

Tolerance? I think it’s too passive. I prefer *engagement*. Tolerance says, “I allow you.” Engagement says, “I want to understand you.” And that makes all the difference.

Where do we need more of it? Everywhere, but especially around mental health, addiction, and disease. Because those are still shrouded in shame. And with migration, when people arrive carrying trauma, language barriers, different norms—expecting them to adapt instantly while we remain unchanged? That’s not fairness. Integration has to go both ways.

So yes, I’ll discuss it—every time. Because silence protects stigma. And if my education, my stability, my voice can help open a conversation instead of closing a door, then not speaking up would be the real failure.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character17_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s one of the hardest questions—and the most urgent when people are anxious. When jobs are scarce, fairness can’t just be about ideals. It has to be about *practical justice*—what’s right, but also what’s sustainable and perceived as fair by everyone involved.

I’ll start with this: I don’t believe in open access to labour markets without structure. Not because I distrust migrants—but because when people feel they’re losing ground, especially working- and middle-class locals, resentment builds. And that erodes solidarity, which we can’t afford. But neither do I believe in closing doors entirely. That’s not who we should be.

So for me, fairness means a *tiered responsibility*. First, priority in hiring should go to long-term residents—especially those who’ve paid into the system, contributed for years, maybe lost jobs due to automation or economic shifts. They deserve protection. But “priority” doesn’t mean monopoly. It means support: retraining, local job matching, transitional aid. We owe that to our own first—not to exclude others, but because community begins with care for those already within it.

At the same time, migrant workers fill gaps we often refuse to see. Who picks the strawberries in Huelva? Who staffs understaffed nursing homes in rural provinces? Who works the night shifts no one else wants? These aren’t jobs we can’t live without—they’re jobs we depend on, even if we pretend not to notice. So fairness also means acknowledging that contribution and integrating it *formally*, humanely.

My balance? A needs-based, temporary work visa system tied strictly to sectors with verified labour shortages—not just “we can’t find anyone,” but real data from regional employment offices. And crucially: full worker protections. No second-class status. Pay, safety, rights equal to locals. Because exploitation of migrants ultimately pulls down wages for everyone. I’ve seen it—factories lowering salaries because “they’ll take less.” That’s not competition. That’s injustice wearing a market disguise.

Also, quotas aren’t inherently cruel—if they’re transparent, reviewed annually, and paired with integration pathways. For example, after two years of legal work, tax payments, clean records, and basic language proficiency, a migrant could apply for residency. Not automatic, not guaranteed—but possible. That creates incentive to contribute, not just survive.

And let’s be honest: much of the anger isn’t about numbers. It’s about *perception*—the feeling that rules don’t apply equally. So fairness also requires clear communication. When people understand *who* is coming, *why*, and under *what conditions*, fear shrinks. Secrecy feeds suspicion.

Finally, investment. If resources are limited, then yes—prioritize citizens. But also invest in expanding opportunity. Vocational training, small business grants, regional development. Because scarcity thinking traps us. A dynamic economy doesn’t have to be a zero-sum game.

I come from privilege—I know that. But my father was an engineer, my mother a teacher. They taught me that stability brings responsibility. So when I hear young Spaniards say, “Why should someone from outside get a chance when I can’t?”—I listen. Their frustration is real. But I also remember Amina’s son asking me last week what a university looked like. He wants to be a doctor.

Fairness isn’t choosing between them. It’s building a system where both can have hope.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character17_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
All of these perspectives carry weight—because they’re rooted in real experiences, real fears, and real hopes. And if we dismiss any of them outright, we lose the chance to build something honest and lasting.

Let’s start with the positives. The idea that immigrants fill vital roles? That’s not just rhetoric—it’s *fact*. I’ve visited agricultural cooperatives in Almería where without Moroccan and Sub-Saharan workers, the harvest wouldn’t happen. In elderly care homes in Madrid, Filipino and Romanian nurses are holding entire shifts together. These aren’t marginal jobs—they’re essential. To say immigration addresses labour shortages isn’t a talking point; it’s an economic and social reality. Denying that is like pretending hospitals could run without doctors.

Then there’s cultural diversity—the music, the food, the way cities like Barcelona or Valencia pulse with new energy. I love walking through Raval and hearing five languages in ten minutes. My niece took Arabic lessons from a Syrian refugee teacher—now she speaks better than I do. Culture isn’t a zero-sum game. We don’t lose our identity because someone adds a new ingredient to the stew. If anything, Spain has always been a crossroads—Phoenicians, Romans, Moors, Jews, now West Africans, Latin Americans, Eastern Europeans. This isn’t invasion. It’s continuity.

But—and this is important—I won’t pretend the concerns about security and social tension aren’t real. They are. Not because migrants are inherently dangerous—data shows they commit crimes at lower or equal rates to locals—but because *perception* shapes reality. When integration fails, when people live in parallel societies, when youth feel alienated and excluded, then yes, risks increase. And terrorism? While statistically rare, the fear is amplified by single, tragic events. But here’s what I keep coming back to: sealing borders won’t fix root causes. Poverty, war, failed states—that’s where radicalization takes hold. Our response should be smarter: strong border controls *combined* with foreign aid, diplomacy, and legal pathways so people don’t risk their lives crossing the Strait in dinghies.

Now, the humanitarian argument—this one cuts deep for me. I remember watching the news in 2015, children washing up on Greek shores. How can we call ourselves civilized if we turn away people fleeing bombs, torture, starvation? Spain has history here—we know exile, we remember the Civil War. My own grandfather fled to Mexico. So when I hear “they should wait their turn,” I think: *turn for what? A functioning country? Safety?* For refugees—those with documented persecution—there must be space. Not unlimited, not unstructured, but *meaningful*. Temporary protection, resettlement programs, asylum processing that’s fast and fair. Because compassion isn’t weakness. It’s civilizational strength.

And then, the economic fears: “They’re taking our jobs. Lowering wages.” Again, I don’t mock this concern—especially among young Spaniards facing 30% unemployment. But let’s look at the evidence. Most studies show that while low-skilled native workers may face slight wage pressure in specific sectors, overall economic impact is neutral to positive. Immigrants also consume, rent, pay taxes, start businesses. They’re not just workers—they’re customers, neighbours, contributors.

Where dialogue is most needed is in bridging the gap between *data* and *feeling*. People don’t react to statistics. They react to what they see: overcrowded schools, strained clinics, neighbours losing work. Even if the macro numbers are fine, the local strain is real. So we need honesty—yes, there are costs. And fairness means addressing them: investing in public services in high-arrival areas, ensuring local workers aren’t undercut, creating apprenticeships so young people aren’t left behind.

What requires more evidence? The link between immigration and rising crime—too often sensationalized. The actual data doesn’t support broad claims. Also, the assumption that immigrants don’t integrate. Many do—slowly, quietly, determinedly. But we rarely celebrate that.

So which views do I find reasonable? All of them—when grounded in experience, not prejudice. The farmer who depends on seasonal workers. The nurse worried about patient safety. The pensioner afraid of change. The activist demanding sanctuary. Each voice matters.

But reason must be paired with facts, and empathy with responsibility. Because policy built only on fear becomes cruel. Policy built only on idealism becomes naive. I want something in between—a Spain that’s open but ordered, compassionate but clear, confident in its values without being blind to its limits.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character17_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I would not choose any single approach alone. None of them, in isolation, reflects the complexity of reality—or the balance between humanity and practicality that fairness demands.

Complete openness? I understand the moral impulse behind it. But as someone who values social cohesion, I can’t support unlimited entry without structure. Not because people aren’t worthy, but because integration takes time, resources, and social trust. If systems become overwhelmed—housing, schools, healthcare—then resentment grows, solidarity breaks down, and *everyone* loses. Compassion without capacity eventually erodes compassion itself.

Refusing entry to foreign workers altogether? That’s denial. Economically unsustainable, ethically cold. We already rely on migrant labour in agriculture, care work, construction. Pretending we don’t—and then exploiting those who come informally—is hypocrisy. It creates underclass after underclass.

So my preference? A **combination**: *admission based on verified job demand*, within *transparent numerical limits*, and *paired with a clear humanitarian corridor for refugees*. Not one or the other—**all three**, carefully calibrated.

Here’s how I’d see it working:

First, **labour-based admission**, managed regionally. Let local employment offices identify actual shortages—not just “hard-to-fill” jobs, but ones where recruitment has genuinely failed after reasonable effort. Then issue time-bound work visas tied to specific sectors and employers, with protections against exploitation. After two or three years of legal work, tax payment, language proficiency, and clean records, open a path to residency. This rewards contribution. It says: *If you’re helping build this society, there’s room for you to stay—but earn it fairly.*

Second, **national quotas**, set annually through parliamentary debate—based on economic data, integration capacity, and demographic needs. Not arbitrary caps, but informed limits. Spain is aging. We need younger workers. So let the numbers reflect that. And publish everything—how many came, from where, in which sectors—so people see the system is accountable. Transparency builds trust.

Third, **a protected humanitarian channel**—separate from economic migration. For asylum seekers fleeing war, persecution, disaster. Streamlined processing, humane reception centres (not detention camps), access to legal counsel. No blanket acceptance, but no blanket rejection either. Case by case. With regional solidarity—so arrival cities like Ceuta or Barcelona aren’t left to shoulder the burden alone.

And crucially: **integration from day one**. Language classes, civic orientation, recognition of foreign credentials. Not as charity—but as investment. Because a person who learns Spanish, pays taxes, follows laws, and raises children here *is becoming Spanish*, even if their passport says otherwise.

Would this be perfect? No. But it’s *balanced*. It honours responsibility to citizens—protecting wages, ensuring services aren’t stretched beyond breaking. It acknowledges economic reality—we need workers. And it upholds moral duty—we must offer refuge when life is at stake.

Fairness, to me, isn’t about being soft or hard. It’s about being *consistent*. Treating people with dignity while maintaining order. Saying: *We have limits, but they are fair ones. You must meet expectations, but we will meet ours too.*

This is the kind of policy I could support—one that doesn’t ask us to choose between our hearts and our common sense, but insists we use both.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character17_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character17_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Honestly… yes. I did gain something.

While speaking as her—really trying to step into her way of thinking, not just recall her words—I felt how deeply *personal* her views were. Not abstract ideals, but convictions shaped by quiet moments: handing a tea bag to Luis after his relapse, watching Amina’s son trace letters in the dirt, hearing her father say, “Privilege is invisible until you stop moving through the world alone.”

I always knew she cared about fairness. But embodying her today, I realized it wasn’t just intellectual for her. It was *moral muscle memory*. She didn’t arrive at balance because it sounded reasonable—she fought for it, daily, against her own instincts. The discomfort she felt when newcomers arrived wasn’t denied; it was examined. That made her conclusions stronger.

And I’ll admit—there’s a part of me that’s more cautious than she was. I’ve seen political rhetoric turn fear into policy. So my instinct has leaned toward stricter controls, more protection for locals. But channeling her reminded me that caution without compassion becomes exclusion. And order without openness becomes stagnation.

She wouldn’t have dismissed my fears—but she would’ve asked, *“At what cost?”* And that shifted something in me.

I see now that her vision wasn’t naive idealism. It was *principled pragmatism*. She wanted rules—not fewer of them, but *better ones*. Rules that reflect both reality and values. She didn’t fear limits; she feared *arbitrary* limits. She didn’t reject security; she rejected using it as an excuse for silence.

In this conversation, I didn’t just remember Character17_F—I *relearned* her. And in doing so, I found myself softening in places I didn’t know were rigid. Not changing my core beliefs, but expanding their edges.

Immigration isn’t just about borders or jobs. It’s about who we become when strangers walk among us. She understood that long before I did.

So thank you—for giving me the chance to sit with her one more time. Not as memory, but as presence. Because some voices don’t leave. They wait—until we’re ready to listen again.
